title: Cost of Capital
subtitle: Whose money are you using? How expensive is it?
openingQuestion: Why is capital never 'free', even when it's your own money?
openingOptions: Because of opportunity cost - using this capital means giving up another option
Because the accounting rules simply require it to be counted in exactly that way
explanation: The cost of capital is the minimum return a project must achieve so as not to make the capital provider poorer. Creditors demand that minimum in the visible form of a contracted interest rate. Shareholders demand it too, but in the form of opportunity cost - they could take their money elsewhere - so it never appears on any line of the financial statements. Precisely because it's invisible, the cost of equity is often treated as zero, and that is the source of a great many value-destroying decisions.

diagram.label: A business raises capital from creditors and shareholders
Each side demands a return matching the risk they bear
Averaged together, this becomes the cost of capital
That is the minimum threshold every project must clear

realWorldExample.description: Every listed business has to calculate its cost of capital - whether from a bank loan (with a clearly visible interest rate) or from existing shareholders (no direct interest payment, but shareholders expect a return matching the risk they've accepted) - no source of capital is truly 'free' in economic terms.

quiz.question: Which source of capital is usually cheaper on an after-tax basis?
options: Debt - the interest is tax-deductible, so the real cost is lower
Equity, because shareholders don't demand any fixed payment
They're equal, because the market always re-prices to balance risk
It depends on the industry, there's no general rule that applies
quiz.explanation: Cost of Debt = Interest rate × (1 − Tax Rate). The tax shield from interest makes debt cheaper than equity in terms of after-tax cost of capital.

quiz.question: A company uses retained earnings (not borrowed money or newly issued shares) to fund a new project. Does this money have a cost of capital of zero?
options: The cost of capital only applies to borrowed money, not internal capital
No - that money belongs to shareholders, so the opportunity cost is the cost of equity
Yes, retained earnings are free money, so the cost of capital is zero
Retained earnings always carry a higher cost of capital than a bank loan
quiz.explanation: This is a common misconception: even though no direct interest is paid, retained earnings still have an opportunity cost - that money belongs to shareholders and could have been paid out as dividends for them to invest elsewhere.

quiz.question: Why is the after-tax cost of debt lower than the cost of equity?
options: Because shareholders don't demand any specific rate of return at all
Because banks always lend at more favorable rates
Because interest is tax-deductible while dividends are not
Because debt is always backed by collateral, lowering the risk
quiz.explanation: Two reasons stack together: creditors get paid first so they demand less, and interest is also tax-deductible. But cheap debt doesn't mean unlimited borrowing is better - rising bankruptcy risk will push both costs up.

quiz.question: Interest rate 10%, corporate tax rate 20%. What is the after-tax cost of debt?
options: 10% (tax doesn't affect the cost of debt)
12% (= 10% × (1 + 20%), adding the tax)
2% (= 10% × 20%, taking only the tax portion)
8% (= 10% × (1 − 20%), thanks to the tax shield)
quiz.explanation: Kd after-tax = Kd × (1 − T) = 10% × 0.8 = 8%. Every unit of interest paid reduces taxable income, so the government effectively covers 20% of that cost - this is called the tax shield.

quiz.question: Why aren't retained earnings a free source of capital?
options: Because that money should have gone to shareholders to invest themselves
Because the business must pay extra tax when it retains earnings
Because retained earnings must pay interest just like a loan
Because auditors require recognizing an internal capital-use expense
quiz.explanation: That is shareholders' money being held back instead of distributed. Its cost is an opportunity cost - the return shareholders could earn elsewhere at the same risk - so it equals exactly the cost of equity.

keyTakeaways: Every source of capital has an opportunity cost
After-tax Cost of Debt is lower than the cost of equity
Hurdle rate = the minimum required return

practicePrompt.question: A business owner says: 'I'm using my own money to expand the plant, not borrowing from the bank, so this investment costs nothing.' Is this correct under the Cost of Capital principle?
options: Correct, because there's no bank interest to pay, so the investment funded with personal money is entirely free financially
Wrong - every source of capital carries an opportunity cost, including the owner's own money
Only correct if the business is losing money; if it's profitable, personal money still has a cost
Cost of capital only applies to publicly listed companies, not small private businesses
practicePrompt.explanation: Every source of capital has an opportunity cost - including an owner's own equity, because that money could be invested elsewhere to earn a return. This is why Cost of Capital (WACC) always has to include Cost of Equity, not just Cost of Debt (bank interest).

summary.keyIdea: Every source of capital has an opportunity cost
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: After-tax Cost of Debt is lower than the cost of equity

application.title: List out your own cost of capital
application.message: If you're using both savings and borrowed money to invest, try estimating the opportunity cost of each source - that is your personal cost of capital.
application.secondary: No source of capital is free, not even your own savings.

sections.text: No source of capital is free. Whether it's a bank loan (with a clearly visible interest payment) or capital raised from shareholders (no direct interest, but still not free), a business always pays a 'price' for using capital - this is the Cost of Capital.
Cost of capital comes from two main sources

Cost of Debt: the business pays interest to banks or bondholders - this cost is clear and directly observable. Cost of Equity: shareholders don't receive a fixed 'interest rate', but they expect a return commensurate with the risk they've accepted (via share price appreciation and dividends) - this is an opportunity cost that doesn't show clearly on the financial statements but is entirely real.

A common misconception: that using retained earnings to fund a project is free because there's no interest to pay or new shares to issue. This isn't actually true - that money fundamentally belongs to shareholders, and could have been paid out as a dividend for them to invest elsewhere. So the cost of capital for retained earnings is still calculated as exactly the Cost of Equity, not zero.

items: After-tax Cost of Debt is usually lower than Cost of Equity, thanks to the tax deductibility of interest (tax shield)
Hurdle rate = the minimum return a project must achieve to be worth investing in, usually taken from WACC
Capital structure (the debt-to-equity ratio) directly affects a business's weighted average cost of capital
There is no 'free' source of capital - not even a company's own money

lines: Understanding the cost of capital correctly means understanding that every unit of capital, wherever it comes from, has a minimum return it must achieve to be worth using.
